messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 40

He is a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his life on the water, and when he talks about the day things changed, he begins with the weather. The sea was rougher than usual, the sky turning dark in a way that made the horizon disappear. His wife had come with him that morning, as she sometimes did, helping sort nets and carrying small supplies while he worked the boat close to shore. He remembers turning to check on her, then hearing the crack of wood and the sudden shift of the deck beneath them. In the confusion, a wave struck the side of the boat and threw her hard against the rail. She did not get back up right away.

He describes the next few minutes as broken into pieces. He is still able to recall the smell of salt, the shouting of other fishermen nearby, the sharp urgency in his own voice as he called her name again and again. She survived, but she was badly injured, and the days after the accident were filled with hospitals, waiting rooms, and the helpless feeling of watching her in pain. Before that day, he understood danger as something that could be managed through experience and skill. Afterward, the sea itself became tied to fear. What had once been work, rhythm, and pride now carried the memory of how quickly life could change.

In the months that followed, he starts sleeping lightly. He wakes before dawn already tense, listening for sounds from the house, sometimes reaching across the bed to make sure his wife is there. He tells himself that he is only being careful, but he notices that his body never fully settles. When rain begins tapping on the roof, he feels his chest tighten. If he hears a boat engine laboring in the distance, his mind goes back to that day so vividly that he can almost feel the deck tilting under his feet. He does not talk much about what happened. In his family, he has long been the one to endure quietly, to work through hardship without drawing attention to himself. So he keeps moving, returning to the boat, mending nets, loading ice, doing what must be done.

He is still a fisherman, though his relationship to the work has changed. He goes out because he has always gone out, because there are bills, because his hands know the tasks better than his words know the feelings. Yet even on calm mornings, he finds himself scanning the water for signs of danger, watching the weather with an intensity that others around him do not always understand. He avoids taking his wife with him, even when she says she is strong enough, and he makes excuses without explaining why. On rough days, he turns back sooner than he used to. He says he is thinking ahead, but he also knows he is trying not to be caught far from shore if something goes wrong again.

At home, he is more irritable than before and sometimes surprised by it. A small comment from his wife can feel like too much, and then he feels ashamed, because she is the person he was trying to protect. He sees her injury as his failure, even though everyone tells him it was an accident. He does not experience that explanation as comfort. Instead, it leaves him feeling as if he should have prevented it if only he had been faster, stronger, or more attentive. He replays the scene often, especially at night, wondering what he might have done differently. The questions never lead anywhere, but they return with the same force each time.

He also notices that he has become less interested in the things that used to give him ease. He still sits with other men at the dock, but he listens more than he speaks. Their laughter sometimes sounds distant to him, as if he is standing just outside a room he once belonged in fully. He keeps himself busy, because stopping gives the memories room to come in. Even so, they come in anyway: in dreams, in flashes when he sees a wave break sharply against the hull, in moments when his body reacts before his mind can explain why.

Now, years later, he remains a steady presence in his family and in the small world of work he knows best, but the accident has not stayed in the past in the way he hoped it would. It lives with him in the boat, in the weather, in the way he looks at his wife when she moves through the house. He carries the memory not as a single event, but as something that continues to shape how he sleeps, how he works, and how closely he watches the people he loves.
